scope_note: Santa Cruz, California is assumed. City, unincorporated county, utility territory, and regional authority are distinct. These are policy-evidence records, not standardized Doughnut scores.

policies.title: Drought rationing and water-waste restrictions
policies.jurisdiction: City of Santa Cruz Water Department service area
policies.scale: Utility service area; not city boundary or whole county
policies.mechanism: Stage 3 emergency, mandatory 25% reduction, restrictions on spray irrigation hours, runoff and hosing hard surfaces.
policies.direction: Observed lower water use; affordability tradeoff unquantified
policies.headline: 26% lower water use
policies.observed_outcomes: Official Attachment 2 reports 26% average monthly savings, alongside residential use of 47 gallons/person/day. Cover text says 28% without matching window; use the explicitly windowed table, not cover figure.
policies.baseline: Same months of 2013; absolute baseline volume not reported in table
policies.counterfactual: Prior year only, not weather-adjusted untreated comparison
policies.design: Supplier administrative reports summarized by County HSA; table visually checked on PDF page 13
policies.costs: Program operating cost not isolated. Contemporary reporting documents utility revenue pressure as reduced sales leave infrastructure costs; no cost-effectiveness estimate.
policies.distribution: Penalties and fixed revenue-recovery charges may burden low-income households; marginal conservation scope differs between efficient households and heavy outdoor users. These distributional mechanisms are not locally quantified.
policies.tradeoffs: Demand reductions protect scarce supply but do not establish ecological streamflow benefits or household wellbeing changes. Drought, publicity, restrictions and price responses cannot be separated.
policies.limitations: Service-area result, not city resident effect. 26% is average monthly savings, not necessarily volume-weighted seasonal savings. No untreated counterfactual. No measured ecological threshold closure.

policies.title: ADU permitting reforms and fee/design assistance
policies.jurisdiction: Unincorporated Santa Cruz County; California enabling/preemptive laws
policies.scale: Unincorporated county, excludes City of Santa Cruz
policies.dates: Local reforms2018,2020–2021; multiple state laws; annual permits2017–2024
policies.mechanism: Ministerial review, eased setbacks/parking, shorter review, fee relief and pre-approved designs lower development barriers.
policies.direction: More permitted units; affordability and completed supply not identified
policies.headline: 28 → 103 ADU permits
policies.observed_outcomes: 2024 General Plan Annual Report Table1:2017 28;2018 37;2019 29;2020 37;2021 63;2022 58;2023 85;2024 103.2024 includes one tiny home on wheels classified as an ADU. This is a permitting output, not completed/occupied units or rent reduction.
policies.counterfactual: No untreated jurisdiction or modeled no-reform trajectory
policies.costs: Report identifies construction and permit costs as barriers; fee reductions and free designs are supports. Total fiscal cost not established. Forgivable Loan Program ended in 2022 for low performance.
policies.distribution: Benefits require property/financing access; potential additional rental or family space is not guaranteed affordable. County removed rent restrictions outside Coastal Zone in2008 and inside in2009.
policies.tradeoffs: Infill can reduce land pressure relative to sprawl but adds water, materials and infrastructure demand. No lifecycle or rent effect measured.
policies.limitations: State/local policy bundle cannot be separated from demand, credit and construction conditions. Use February2025 General Plan report Table1 full-year series; source explicitly includes one tiny home on wheels among2024 ADUs.

policies.title: Youth Cruz Free fares
policies.scale: Regional county-serving transit authority, not City policy
policies.dates: Pilot began March1 2023; survey May29–August15 2024; report August2025
policies.mechanism: Fare-free local buses remove a monetary access barrier for school-age youth.
policies.direction: Observed transit uptake; educational and climate effects unmeasured
policies.headline: 31% of respondents started riding
policies.headline_window: Recalled pre-March2023 vs during pilot, survey2024
policies.observed_outcomes: 86/280 respondents reported riding only after pilot began; 136/280 rode in both periods; 33/280 stopped;25/280 never rode. Agency also reported536% youth ridership growth, but accessible summary lacks raw denominator/time window, so do not use that as the main metric.
policies.baseline: Respondents' recalled bus use before March1 2023
policies.design: UC Davis observational survey:394 usable cases overall;280 for Table1. School/network recruitment, not representative probability sample.
policies.costs: December2024 board report records $1,192,777 LCTOP award for continuation of free/reduced fares, with confirmation of Youth Cruz Free funding being pursued. Grant award is not total program cost or expenditure.
policies.distribution: Fare removal supports youth without cars; survey associations with ethnicity, vehicle access and safety suggest benefits/access are uneven. Rural and communities-of-color representation requires improvement.
policies.tradeoffs: Fare-free service requires stable replacement funding and sufficient service. New bus trips need not replace car trips; cannot infer CO2 savings. No causal school-attendance result.
policies.limitations: Recall/selection bias, no control group, pandemic recovery and service changes. 31% is new rider share, not ridership growth. Age-related driving access changes travel behavior.

sources.title: Pike et al. Youth Cruz Free, UC Davis/NCST August2025, Table1 p10

policies.title: Source-separated food-scrap collection
policies.jurisdiction: City of Santa Cruz implementing California AB1826 and SB1383
policies.dates: Commercial pilot byFY2018; preprocessing2019; residential rollout2022; City newsletter2023
policies.mechanism: Separate food scraps from landfill waste and process for secondary uses; residential and commercial collection.
policies.direction: Measured diversion output; net emissions/nutrient effects not measured
policies.headline: About40 tons diverted weekly
policies.headline_unit: tons of food waste per week
policies.observed_outcomes: FY2018 report:45–50 tons/month from commercial collection serving over26 businesses. City2023 newsletter:about40 tons/week from residential+commercial. Changed service population means these are rollout milestones, not like-for-like efficacy estimates.
policies.baseline: FY2018 commercial pilot45–50tons/month; not a matched baseline
policies.counterfactual: No measured no-program disposal trajectory; city's diverted-from-landfill accounting
policies.costs: Capital/operating cost not established from primary sources reviewed. Do not calculate net fiscal savings from throughput.
policies.distribution: Rollout newsletter says multifamily complexes not yet enrolled could use drop-off; convenience differed by housing type. Current mandatory service applies all housing types.
policies.tradeoffs: Transport and processing consume energy; feedstock recovery is not edible food redistribution. Biogas at City's wastewater plant was future work in2023, not a demonstrated benefit then.
policies.limitations: No measured methane avoided, lifecycle emissions, food security improvement or nutrient runoff effect. Do not annualize40tons/week as observed annual tonnage or confuse with county's broader organics totals.

policies.title: Community-choice electricity procurement (3CE)
policies.jurisdiction: Central Coast Community Energy multi-jurisdiction JPA
policies.scale: Regional electricity supplier; not a Santa Cruz-only outcome
policies.dates: Operations since2018;2024 rate comparison;2025 power-content label published2026
policies.mechanism: Publicly governed generation procurement, renewable contracts and opt-up tariff; PG&E still delivers electricity.
policies.direction: Mixed: modeled tariff saving; default supply emissions intensity above state comparator
policies.headline: 551 vs384 lbCO2e/MWh
policies.headline_window: 2025, 3CE total vs CA utility-average total, same scope
policies.observed_outcomes: 2025 label: 3CE total intensity551 vs California utility-average total384 lbCO2e/MWh (retail sales, other end uses and losses). Retail-only3Cchoice542;3Cprime0. These are accounting intensities, not marginal or causal avoided emissions.
policies.baseline: Contemporaneous statewide total benchmark384, not untreated Santa Cruz counterfactual
policies.counterfactual: No causal no-CCA comparison. Tariff illustration compares matched375kWh usage at published2024 rates.
policies.design: CEC power-source disclosure accounting; joint3CE/PG&E tariff illustration
policies.costs: 2024 E-TOU-C illustration at375kWh/month:PG&E$172.57 vs3Cchoice$158.71, modeled$13.86/month (~8.0%) difference including delivery/PCIA. Not measured household savings, not current2026 rates, and rate effective dates differ (PG&EJune1;3CEJan1).
policies.distribution: Benefits vary with tariff, usage, vintage fees and eligibility. Cheap generation alone does not remove delivery charges. No local energy-poverty effect identified.
policies.tradeoffs: New renewable contracts can have additionality benefits but procurement accounting does not prove them. Offsite land/material and grid effects require lifecycle evidence. A100%renewable opt-up product is not default service.
policies.limitations: Do not use regional energy totals as Santa Cruz city effects.2025 new reporting separates retail-only and total scopes:compare total551 with total384, not retail542 with state-total384. No automatic climate-success label.
